ignoreNoise.title: Do not confuse fresh highs with broad conviction.

briefingContext.essentialIntro: This is one tight daily edition. Read the pulse first, then work the story cards top to bottom for a full 15 to 20 minute briefing.

peerMiss.title: The real bridge story is energy, not the loudest macro headline.
peerMiss.body: A lot of people will narrate the day around central banks or a single earnings print. The more useful frame is that energy is connecting geopolitics, inflation risk, and equity fragility underneath almost everything else.

sayInMeeting.title: Use this line.
sayInMeeting.body: The market is not ignoring risk; it is temporarily outsourcing that risk to oil, yields, and a narrow group of index leaders.

chartOfDay.title: Index highs versus breadth health.
chartOfDay.body: Compare fresh cap-weighted highs with equal-weight participation. If the index keeps climbing while breadth stalls, the rally is stronger on paper than underneath.
chartOfDay.takeaway: The chart is not about being bearish. It is about knowing whether optimism is broad or rented from a handful of names.

deepDive.title: Why oil is the connector theme.
deepDive.body: Energy is what turns a regional headline into an inflation question, a rates question, and then a valuation question for the rest of the tape.
deepDive.whyNow: If you miss that bridge, the day feels random when it is actually much more connected.

footerPerspective.title: The durable frame is that the market still wants to be bullish, but it is paying more hidden rent than the headline makes obvious.
footerPerspective.summary: That rent is being paid through energy, narrow leadership, and a world backdrop that keeps threatening to become more expensive. If you carry that frame into the day, most of the noise gets easier to sort.

candidates.headline: Policy week and megacap earnings are hitting the market at the same time.
candidates.takeaway: This is not a normal wait-for-the-Fed tape. Macro and micro risk are arriving together, which means the market has fewer places to hide if confidence slips.
candidates.whatChanged: Bloomberg framed the week as a collision between central-bank decisions and heavyweight earnings, compressing a lot of narrative risk into a very short window.
candidates.whyItMatters: The market is not dealing with one driver. It is balancing policy, valuation, leadership concentration, and earnings credibility all at once.
candidates.marketImpact: If results are merely fine, the rally can stay intact. If one of the major leadership pillars wobbles, downside can travel faster than the calm tape suggests.
candidates.disagreement: Bulls read the setup as proof that demand for quality and AI leadership can absorb bad news. Bears think the calm mostly reflects concentration and pre-positioning, not broad conviction.
candidates.watchToday: Any pre-earnings tone shift, futures sensitivity to macro headlines, and whether cyclicals participate instead of just tagging along.

candidates.headline: Oil is doing more macro work than the index headline suggests.
candidates.takeaway: Right now energy is not a side story. It is the hinge that connects world news, inflation nerves, and what central banks may or may not feel comfortable saying next.
candidates.whatChanged: Multiple reports kept crude and regional shipping risk near the center of the macro setup while equities tried to stay composed.
candidates.whyItMatters: If oil stays elevated into a central-bank-heavy week, the market has less room to keep pretending disinflation is automatic.
candidates.marketImpact: Energy can stay bid, long-duration assets get more fragile, and any rate-sensitive growth trade becomes harder to defend at rich valuations.
candidates.disagreement: Optimists think each diplomatic headline can cap crude quickly. Skeptics think shipping risk keeps a sticky premium in the system even when the news flow cools temporarily.
candidates.watchToday: Brent behavior, Hormuz diplomacy, and whether yields react more to crude than to central-bank messaging.

candidates.headline: Powell's final meeting as chair turned into a Fed-handoff story.
candidates.takeaway: The rate decision mattered less than the split around it and Powell's choice to remain on the board, because both now shape how investors will read the handoff to Kevin Warsh.
candidates.whatChanged: Bloomberg and Reuters both emphasized two things at once: a more divided Fed decision and Powell's decision to stay on as a governor after May 15.
candidates.whyItMatters: This is now a succession story as much as a rates story. The market has to price not just the next policy move, but how much independence and continuity the post-Powell Fed will project.
candidates.marketImpact: Treasury yields, rate-cut expectations, and policy-sensitive equities can all stay jumpy because the leadership transition is now part of the macro risk map.
candidates.disagreement: Some investors will read Powell staying on as a stabilizer. Others will read the dissents and the handoff itself as proof that policy uncertainty is getting harder to contain.
candidates.watchToday: How yields behave after the meeting, whether Warsh expectations shift, and whether equity leadership still acts like the Fed backdrop is benign.

candidates.headline: Fresh index highs are still masking thinner leadership than the headline implies.
candidates.takeaway: The market can look healthy at the index level while becoming more fragile underneath. That distinction matters more than the celebratory headline.
candidates.whatChanged: The Wall Street Journal market coverage pointed to strong index-level performance led by a relatively small set of dominant names.
candidates.whyItMatters: When headline strength outruns breadth, the market can feel more stable than it really is. That reduces the margin for disappointment.
candidates.marketImpact: If leadership broadens, bulls gain a sturdier foundation. If it narrows further, any pullback can feel sudden and disproportionately sharp.
candidates.disagreement: Some investors see concentration as a natural feature of an AI-led cycle. Others see it as a warning that passive index strength is hiding weaker internals.
candidates.watchToday: Breadth, equal-weight performance, and whether non-megacap sectors confirm the move instead of just watching it happen.

candidates.headline: The UK-US diplomatic theater matters because symbolic alignment can become policy alignment.
candidates.takeaway: A ceremonial visit does not move markets on its own, but it can matter if it stabilizes expectations around allied coordination when the geopolitical backdrop is already tense.
candidates.whatChanged: Associated Press framed King Charles III's Washington visit and address to Congress as an effort to emphasize continuity in the UK-US relationship.
candidates.whyItMatters: When geopolitical coordination is in focus, symbolic reassurance can reduce uncertainty around trade, security alignment, and allied posture.
candidates.marketImpact: The direct market effect is limited, but the broader diplomatic tone can shape how investors think about policy coordination during a risk-heavy week.
candidates.disagreement: Some people dismiss this as pure symbolism. Others see symbolism as useful when policy relationships need visible reinforcement.
candidates.watchToday: Any concrete policy or trade messaging that turns the symbolism into something more actionable.
